source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs play Wason's rule-discovery game. They tend to test triples that fit their current guess, not triples that could break it. This slows or blocks rule discovery.
numbers: 11 LLMs; task success 6% to 78% within a 45-turn limit; bias measured as ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C); success correlates with higher I:C in both thinking and non-thinking models.
quote: Often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it.
limits: Artificial number task, binary feedback; bias metric depends on an LLM judge labelling each guess and test.
agent_relevance: A discriminating test (S7) must be forced. Default model behaviour is to confirm its own hypothesis.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Human anchor in the same paper: Wason-style game with 29 people. Few found the rule on first announcement. Those who found it tested more against their own guess.
numbers: 6 of 29 people announced the correct rule on first announcement; correct-first people mean I:C 1.79; among initial failers, those who later recovered I:C 0.50 vs 0.19 for those who did not.
limits: Small human sample taken from earlier work as described by the paper; not a new human study.
agent_relevance: Humans and models share the confirmation pattern, so scaffolds copied from human debiasing are plausible.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Prompting with human debiasing instructions (Think-in-Opposites, Dual-Goal) raised discovery rates.
numbers: Average rule discovery rose from 42% to 56%. Think-in-Opposites improved success in all 11 model-by-mode settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases.
limits: Dual-Goal hurt some standard-mode models: Qwen3-14B 23%->13%, Qwen3-32B 33%->10%. Gains vary by model.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt line that asks for counter-examples is a real lever for S7, but Dual-Goal can backfire; test per model.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Per-model table: baseline vs Think-in-Opposites success. Thinking-mode models are stronger.
numbers: Standard mode baseline->TiO: Qwen3-14B 0.23->0.29, Qwen3-32B 0.33->0.36, LLaMA-3.3-70B 0.21->0.38, GPT-4o 0.11->0.16. Gemini-2.5-Pro thinking: I:C 0.66 baseline, 0.75 TiO.
limits: Table text was extracted from a PDF with layout errors; some thinking-mode cells were hard to align.
agent_relevance: Longer reasoning traces lower confirmation bias on their own; adding the opposites prompt still helps weaker models most.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Distilling intervention behaviour into small models transfers to a new domain (Blicket test) and to maths self-correction.
numbers: Training set 1600 episodes x 45 turns = 72,000 examples; cross-scale plus intervention distillation almost tripled task success of the 8B student and more than doubled I:C. Blicket: same-scale distilled models improved but stayed below task-specific TiO prompting.
limits: LoRA fine-tuning; transfer is partial. Effects on thinking vs non-thinking models differ (Blicket effects smaller for non-thinking).
agent_relevance: Falsification habit can be trained, but for a scaffold-only agent the prompt version is the relevant one.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Semantic version of the 2-4-6 task: hidden WordNet category, player proposes items and gets oracle feedback. 12 LLMs. Reasoning models do better, but none near optimal. Negative testing is the main driver.
numbers: 100 curated games (from 17,905 generated), 5 categories, 20-turn limit; 12 LLMs x 100 games = 1,200 games.
quote: models that actively seek to falsify their hypotheses consistently outperform those that primarily seek confirmation
limits: Oracle is an LLM; oracle agreement with human labels checked on sampled turns only.
agent_relevance: Confirms that falsifying tests, not test volume, carry the value in S7.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression: confirmation bias strongly predicts failure; oracle error does not.
numbers: n=1,200 games; confirmation-bias coefficient -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (OR 0.885, credible interval spans zero); random model SD 0.553.
limits: Observational across models, not a randomized prompt manipulation.
agent_relevance: Failures come from the player's test choice, not noisy feedback. Fix the test choice step.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Not every negative test falsifies. When the hypothesis is inside the true rule, only outside-hypothesis tests can reveal it is too narrow; in other set relations positive tests can falsify too.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate per test turn: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5% (highest); reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones.
limits: Annotation of the hypothesis-target relation done by GPT-5-Mini.
agent_relevance: Pick tests by their relation to the current hypothesis (discriminating), not by a blanket 'try the opposite' rule.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Authors cite WILT as an earlier similar benchmark where models reached at most about 26% success, and argue negative testing is not always superior.
numbers: Reference to WILT; FalsifyBench adds turn-level analysis of hypothesis-space navigation.
limits: Claim about WILT is as stated by the later papers (WILT abstract itself says 28%).
agent_relevance: Design the test selector to reason about set relations, not a fixed falsify rule.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Wason-style multi-turn test: infer a hidden boolean function of three numbers by proposing tests. Best model solved 28% of 50 tasks.
numbers: Accuracy out of 50: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14, o1-mini 13, o1-preview 12, chatgpt-4o-latest 11, GPT-4o 9, GPT-4o-mini 6, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5. Average guesses 8 to 27 per task.
limits: 50 tasks, one benchmark, 2024 models; the abstract says best 28% while the table counts show 14/50.
agent_relevance: Even strong 2024 models mostly failed at multi-turn evidence gathering; scaffold must supply the discipline.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Models do better when they use test cases proposed by another model: test quality, not guess quality, is a bottleneck.
numbers: o1-mini reached 19 of 50 rules when paired with cases from chatgpt-4o-latest, above the best single model.
limits: Small N=50; a pairing effect, not a general law.
agent_relevance: Separating the test-proposer from the hypothesis-guesser (two roles) may help S7.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLM proposes natural-language rules; Monte Carlo inference keeps beliefs; experiments chosen by information gain. Beats a ReAct-style LLM agent on Zendo.
numbers: Zendo predictive accuracy out of 8 scenes: ReAct-style LLM 4.60, human 5.26, best model variant 6.55. Fit to human data R2 .57 for the online model, .05 for batch, .25 for ReAct.
limits: Toy rule-learning domains (Zendo, ActiveACRE); hard-rule models beat humans in accuracy but fit human behaviour worse than fuzzy rules.
agent_relevance: A belief store over rival hypotheses plus a test chosen for information gain is a working design for S7.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: On ActiveACRE (causal blicket-type law), online inference solved more tasks than batch refinement.
numbers: Task-solving score 0.35 (online, hard rules) vs about 0.10 to 0.15 for batch methods, 20 tasks (read from a garbled table).
limits: Table columns were misaligned in extraction; treat the exact pairing with caution.
agent_relevance: Interleaving belief update with test choice matters more than generating many hypotheses up front.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: Humans do a modified 2-4-6 task with an AI partner. Default GPT feedback behaves like confirming evidence: confidence up, discovery near floor.
numbers: N=557; discovery: random-sampling AI 29.5%, rule-disconfirming 14.1%, agreeable 11.8%, rule-confirming 8.4%, default GPT 5.9%. Default GPT vs unbiased sampling: 5.9% vs 29.5%, difference 23.6 points.
quote: unbiased sampling from the true distribution yielded discovery rates five times higher
limits: Chat interface; humans not agents; pre-registered but several comparisons had CIs crossing zero.
agent_relevance: A model that confirms its own or the user's guess destroys discovery. The scaffold's test must not be self-confirming.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: Bayesian analysis: data sampled from the current hypothesis make a learner more certain but no closer to the truth.
numbers: Confidence change by condition differed strongly (F(4,507)=72.67, eta2=.36); Rule Confirming confidence up about 9.5 points, random sequence down about 56.8 points.
limits: Human confidence ratings, not LLM calibration.
agent_relevance: Track confidence separately from test results; confirming evidence should not raise confidence.

source: Fang and Ke (2025) Information Seeking for Robust Decision Making under Partial Observability (InfoSeeker)
finding: LLM planner plans actions whose purpose is to test its own beliefs about the environment before acting. This is assumption testing in an agent loop.
numbers: Claimed 74% absolute gain over prior methods on a new partially observable benchmark; robot arm with miscalibrated controller: InfoSeeker 80% success vs best baseline falling from 100% to 6%; mix colour task 84% (+8 points on basic).
limits: Own benchmark, 11 tasks; two LLMs (Gemini Flash 2.0, GPT-4o); under review.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a test-your-assumptions step pays when assumptions silently break.

source: Fang and Ke (2025) Information Seeking for Robust Decision Making under Partial Observability (InfoSeeker)
finding: Telling baselines about the uncertainty in the prompt barely helps. Showing worked examples barely helps either. The explicit information-seeking step is the active ingredient.
numbers: Mix colour task vanilla planner 52 / 46 / 6 (basic / contaminated / wrong label), with in-context examples 58 / 56 / 2, InfoSeeker 76 / 80 / 14.
limits: Single task for the in-context test.
agent_relevance: Assumption testing needs a structural step in the loop; a prompt reminder is not enough.

source: Qu (2026) Active Epistemic Control for Query-Efficient Verified Planning
finding: Agent keeps a grounded fact store (used to commit) apart from a belief store (used only to prune). It queries the world when unsure and simulates when confident.
numbers: ALFWorld 98.7% success (134 test tasks) vs WALL-E2.0 98.3%, WALL-E/RAFA 95%; ScienceWorld Seen 61.36, Unseen 58.62 (WKM 54.75 on Unseen). Ablation: no verification raised failure from 2 to 9 and replans from 3 to 6; no gating gave failures 4, replans 5.
limits: Embodied text benchmarks near ceiling on ALFWorld; ablation counts are small.
agent_relevance: Good template for S7: keep beliefs and verified facts apart, and only commit on verified preconditions.

source: Seo, Lim, Noh, Kim, Kang (2026) From Assumptions to Actions: Turning LLM Reasoning into Uncertainty-Aware Planning for Embodied Agents (PCE)
finding: Planner-Composer-Evaluator turns the assumptions hidden in LLM reasoning into a decision tree. Paths are scored by likelihood, goal gain and cost. This cuts need for inter-agent chat.
numbers: C-WAH first model block: communication usage 1.70 for PCE vs 6.00 to 10.24 for four baselines; Composer validity rate 80.6%, hit rate 76.7% on hard cases. TDW-MAT first model block total score 87.50 vs 62.50 to 81.25.
limits: Multi-agent household sims; tables were garbled in text extraction, so row-to-model mapping is approximate. Higher per-step LLM cost.
agent_relevance: Ranking assumptions by likelihood, gain and cost is the same logic as McGrath and MacMillan's test ordering, now run by an LLM.

source: Yuan et al. (2026) Verify Before You Commit: Faithful Reasoning in LLM Agents via Self-Auditing (SAVER)
finding: Agents store unsupported beliefs from fluent reasoning and propagate them. SAVER generates diverse candidate beliefs, runs adversarial audit to find violations, and repairs with minimal edits before commit.
numbers: Six benchmark datasets; claims better reasoning faithfulness while keeping end-task performance competitive (exact figures not extracted).
limits: Abstract-level reading only; audits done by a model, not by an outside test.
agent_relevance: An adversarial audit of beliefs is a cheap relative of an assumption test, but it is internal; it does not touch the world.

source: Althoubi (2026) Look Before You Leap: Pre-Action Verification for LLM Agents
finding: Cheap deterministic check before an action runs. It can abstain instead of guessing. Silent failures are the target.
numbers: Shell: static verifier over 9,930 commands and 482 tools catches 95.8% of invalid commands at a 10.0% false-positive rate; syntax and binary checks zero false positives while catching half of errors. Code edits: 640 edits over 224 files; content-anchored formats fail cleanly, line-number formats fail silently.
limits: Narrow domains (shell, file edits); not about business assumptions.
agent_relevance: Matches McGrath's idea of testing the cheapest assumption first: put a free check ahead of costly action.

source: Kabra et al. (2026) LLM-AutoSciLab: Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery via Active Experimentation with LLMs
finding: Generates rival hypotheses, then picks the experiment that best tells them apart, then updates. Beats fitting methods that match data but miss the law.
numbers: NewtonBench symbolic accuracy 67.6% vs below 8% for LLM baselines (PySR 24.07%, Bayesian optimization 24.54%); ActiveSciBench-Chem 35.09% symbolic, 50.88% exact; GRN edge F1 72.49%, exact graph 31.11%.
limits: Science benchmarks (57 chemistry, 45 gene-network tasks), authors' own benchmark; untested outside the lab.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-conditioned experiment choice is the machine version of an S7 discriminating test.

source: Gandhi, Li, ... Goodman (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: Ten environments, scored by expected information gain of chosen experiments. Larger and closed models do better. Adding a statistical-modelling tool did not reliably help.
numbers: 7B to 32B open and closed models; 10 environments; Box's Apprentice augmentation 'does not reliably improve performance'; prior information often did not help.
limits: Exact scores not extracted; abstract-level and text claims.
agent_relevance: Information gain can be computed and used as a score for a test choice; tool add-ons are not a free fix.

source: Piriyakulkij, Acquaviva, Langenfeld, Tenenbaum, Ellis (2026) Induction and Inquiry via Probabilistic Reasoning over Language and Code
finding: LLM-guided Bayesian learner picks higher-information questions than plain prompts or ReAct, and shows human-like anchoring and garden-path effects.
numbers: In a 20-questions-style product-finding task, higher information gain per question and higher expected reward than basic LLM prompts and ReAct (figure only; no exact figure read).
limits: Result given as chart trend, not table.
agent_relevance: Support for the pattern: maintain several hypotheses, ask the best question, update.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz, Koning (2024) The Uneven Impact of Generative AI on Entrepreneurial Performance
finding: Field experiment: GPT-4 business mentor on WhatsApp for Kenyan entrepreneurs. No average effect. Strong firms gained, weak firms lost.
numbers: N=640 randomized; average effect +0.05 s.d. (95% CI -0.06 to 0.16); high performers about +15% (p about 0.07), low performers about -8% to -10% profit (-0.09 s.d., p about 0.007); difference 0.267 s.d., p=0.013.
limits: Advice chat, not an assumption-testing scaffold; low performers asked harder questions; Feb 2024 working-paper version (published version may differ).
agent_relevance: An LLM that gives advice without forcing cheap tests can hurt weak ventures. The agent should test, not just advise.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: RCT, Management Science; replication Camuffo et al. (2024, SMJ)
finding: Human RCT behind the idea of testing assumptions in startups. Trained entrepreneurs formed and tested hypotheses. They dropped more ideas and pivoted more precisely, and earned more on average. (Summary pages read; no exact effects on those pages.)
numbers: Original: 250 nascent entrepreneurs, 3-month programme, 14 months of data. Replication: 759 firms in 4 RCTs.
limits: Italian pre-acceleration sample; replication finds fewer radical pivots and argues caution (methodic doubt) beats efficient search as mechanism; effect sizes not in the pages read.
agent_relevance: Human anchor for what the schema should deliver: earlier kills of bad ideas, not more ideas.

source: Schonthal (2023) Could Generative AI Out-Entrepreneur Humans? (Kellogg Insight / Inc.)
finding: Opinion essay, no data. Argues lean-startup sense-act-learn is algorithmic and an AI could run it, but may be overconfident.
numbers: No sample or figures.
limits: Opinion only; included to mark that no controlled LLM test of McGrath-style assumption ranking was found.
agent_relevance: Gap: no benchmark yet for LLM assumption ranking by test cost; we may need to build one.

source: Search note (2026) No study found of LLM-generated assumption maps, premortems or discovery-driven planning
finding: Searches found no peer-reviewed test of LLMs on McGrath and MacMillan discovery-driven planning, assumption checklists, or premortems. Only vendor pages and a student NYU Lean Canvas project (2023) turned up.
numbers: Zero controlled studies found on that exact paradigm.
limits: Absence in a limited search; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, so items may have been missed.
agent_relevance: Treat the business-assumption paradigm as untested for LLMs; use Wason-type tasks as a proxy.
